title: Scarcity: Why Having Too Little Means So Much
research_question: Does the subjective experience of having less than one feels one needs causally shape cognitive functioning and decision-making, thereby producing self-reinforcing patterns of behavior across domains such as poverty, loneliness, dieting, and time pressure? Specifically, does lacking a resource impose a cognitive burden that reduces problem-solving capacity and self-control, leading individuals to make choices that deepen their own deprivation?
data_description: The book synthesizes findings from multiple behavioral studies. Cited evidence includes a wartime starvation study in which volunteers were gradually deprived of food over several months and tracked for psychological consequences; laboratory tasks in which participants stratified by income considered hypothetical car-repair expenses of $300 versus $3000 and then completed intelligence tests; a field study of Indian sugarcane farmers tested on cognitive tasks before harvest (cash-poor) and after harvest (cash-rich); and a memorization experiment in which participants memorized two-digit versus seven-digit numbers and then chose between fruit and cake. Additional evidence cited includes data on U.S. air-traffic controllers' parenting behavior on high-traffic days. Key variables span fluid intelligence, executive control, impulsive choice, borrowing behavior, and parenting quality.
institutional_context: The work sits within behavioral economics, building on Kahneman, Tversky, and Thaler. The motivating setting is the universal human condition of resource shortage — whether of money, time, food, or social connection — and how it manifests across very different populations: the chronically poor in developing and developed countries, dieters, lonely individuals, busy professionals, and farmers with seasonal income. A central illustrative setting is the agricultural cycle of Indian sugarcane farmers, whose income arrives in a lump sum at harvest, creating predictable within-person variation between periods of financial strain and relative abundance. Other settings include American workplaces with automatic retirement enrollment and consumers facing late-payment penalties, which motivate policy designs that accommodate the cognitive limits imposed by scarcity rather than relying on traditional incentives.
